summary.register_caveat: Initial 88-item/zero-open validation predates these findings. The owner registered three defects at 2026-09-05T02:20:00Z; the reconciled register validates with 91 items and 3 open repairs.

findings.title: A delayed commit can make the immutable availability clock earlier than database visibility
findings.observed: The worker samples UTC+10 seconds before inserting receipts and committing. A deterministic miniature-database reproduction used the production now=None branch and an 11-second virtual commit delay: availability=13:15:12, actual commit=13:15:13; a separate read-only connection saw zero receipts immediately before commit. Final worker status=ok and the canonical checker returned ok=true with zero optimistic/operational clock violations.
findings.expected: A claimed operational availability time must never precede durable visibility of the evidence. Integrity must verify this bound independently, not only compare the claim with raw first_seen or with a view that repeats the same claim.
findings.impact: A later replay can credit source information earlier than it actually became usable. Research causal timestamps may be optimistic during long transactions. The reproduction does not establish that any historical production receipt experienced such a delay, that a forecast used it, or that an order occurred.
findings.next_step: Design an append-only commit/publication attestation whose causal timestamp is taken after durable commit and whose visibility is required by consumers. Add a virtual slow-commit regression and an independent-clock verification. Inspect existing commit/publication traces before determining historical impact; do not rewrite immutable receipts or award retroactive proof credit.
findings.verification: Offline virtual-clock fixture, real miniature SQLite visibility, no real sleep/network/production database.

findings.title: Normal in-progress publication replaces the only completed integrity snapshot
findings.observed: Every ordinary run overwrites the completed state JSON with status=building and no next_scan_cursor_utc, committed receipt counts or transaction_committed field. The consumer requires status=ok, valid cutoff and committed state. A miniature fixture proved that the previous committed state passed the exact checker, while the actual captured building publication failed on the same healthy database. The saved 2026-09-05T01:45:33Z audit exhibits this exact field pattern: state cutoff=null, state receipt count=0 and database count=9991.
findings.expected: Progress telemetry must not replace the completed state consumed as an integrity attestation. A normal, bounded transaction should not look like broken committed evidence solely because a reader sampled its progress phase.
findings.impact: False degraded publications, noisy or unavailable operational attestation and prolonged ambiguity if shutdown/crash freezes a building state. This is fail-closed, not an execution-authority bypass; the saved mismatch alone does not prove database corruption.
findings.next_step: Separate heartbeat/progress publication from the last completed state or explicitly capture/retry a completed snapshot under a bounded contract. Keep freshness and real failure checks strict. Add interleaved producer/consumer regression coverage and preserve the historical degraded audit.
findings.verification: Deterministic offline miniature database; accepted committed snapshot versus rejected captured building snapshot.

findings.title: A retry loses the progressed scan cursor and replays from activation
findings.observed: Resume accepts prior scan_started_utc only when prior status=ok. Input-lock, database-error and building publications overwrite that file with a non-ok status. A fixture progressed to13:15:32, injected an input lock or registry lock, then retried: the next actual article query began at13:15:00 activation and reread an already processed article. An interrupted building publication produces the same reset. Receipt deduplication kept new_receipt_count=0.
findings.expected: A retry or process interruption must preserve the last committed cursor without advancing past unread rows or resetting to the beginning of the entire cohort.
findings.impact: Repeated historical scans after transient locks or interruption increase latency and shared-registry contention and can widen collection delays. No skipped row or duplicated immutable receipt was observed in the fixture.
findings.next_step: Persist the last committed cursor independently of progress/error status, validate its cohort and activation bounds, and resume from that checkpoint. Add a progressed-success -> error -> second-run test for both input and registry errors and interrupted building state.
findings.verification: Offline actual run transitions with mocked failures and miniature fixture rows. Existing lock test covers only the first failed cycle from activation, not the next cycle after a progressed cursor.

verification.pytest_environment: Python3.13; PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1; PYTHONPATH canonical root plus trad; temporary fixtures, cacheprovider disabled.
verification.custom_regressions: Three deterministic miniature-database scenarios, including input/registry/interrupted-building cursor variants. Canonical checker and helpers AST-extracted; worker/governance imported without runtime main. Temporary databases only, no network, active ledger scans or real sleep.
verification.limitations: Passing tests validate only their asserted behavior. The new fixtures expose gaps in existing tests; tests, hashes and recreation do not prove that all software is bug-free.
verification.reproduction_exit_semantics: Exit 0 means diagnostic completed, not healthy or repaired code. All three known defects reproduced.
